text:
# The Membrane

The building had been designed, in 1968, by a man who believed concrete was a moral substance. Hollister Hall rose from the eastern edge of the quad in four cantilevered tiers, each wider than the one below, so that from a distance it resembled a stack of books someone had set down in a hurry. Students called it the Bunker. The Department of Comparative Literature, which had occupied its upper two floors since the Nixon administration, called it nothing at all, the way one doesn't name the weather.

It was Helen Marsh, a scholar of the Portuguese baroque, who first understood that something was wrong. She had been in her fourth-floor office for twenty-two years, long enough to outlive three office chairs and one marriage, and that spring she noticed that the spines of her books on the lowest shelf had begun to bloom, faintly green, faintly white, soft as the skin of a peach. She pulled out a volume of Vieira's sermons and found its pages fused into a single block, which she held in both hands, as if it were a small animal that had died.

Facilities sent a man with a moisture meter, who pressed its prongs against the wall beneath her window and watched the needle swing hard right and stay there.

"Huh," he said.

By September, a building envelope study had produced a finding so simple no one could believe it. Hollister Hall had no waterproofing membrane. The architect's drawings specified one: a bituminous layer, three-eighths of an inch thick, between the structural concrete and the exterior cladding. The contractor in 1969 had simply not installed it. Whether this was oversight, economy, or revenge against the architect, who was by all accounts insufferable, would never be known.

For fifty-four years, then, rain had been entering the building, moving through the concrete a millimeter a season. It had rusted the rebar, swollen the plaster, and fed a population of organisms the report described, with what Helen thought was unnecessary relish, as "robust."

The chair, a Dante scholar named Peter Lindqvist, read the report aloud at the October faculty meeting, in the voice he used for the Inferno.

"So we've been living in a sponge," said Arnold Feeney, who taught the Russians and was seventy-nine.

"A very well-regarded sponge," Peter said. "It's in two architecture textbooks."

---

Repairs were to begin in January and end in August. Helen pinned the project schedule to the corkboard outside her office, where it acquired annotations. *Ha*, someone wrote beside "Phase 2: Exterior Cladding Removal (6 wks)." Beside "Phase 4: Membrane Installation," someone had drawn a small, careful unicorn.

The university did not move the department. The dean, a former economist who described all problems as "challenges of sequencing," explained that relocation could not be justified "in the present fiscal environment." Classes would continue. Life, the dean wrote, would continue.

It did, in a fashion.

Scaffolding went up, enclosing the building like a cage around a large and sullen bird. The windows were covered with white plastic that admitted a diffuse, sourceless light, the light inside a cloud. Helen began keeping a small clock on her bookshelf because she wanted to see the hands move.

Then came the noise. The steel anchors holding the panels had to be cut with a tool that produced a grinding shriek, as though the building were being asked a question it found unbearable. It traveled through the concrete, up through the floor and into the spine. Arnold said it was like living inside a dentist's drill, then said that was too easy: it was like living inside the toothache itself.

The graduate students fled and did not come back. Helen taught Camões with the door closed and found she had to shout the lines (*Alma minha gentil, que te partiste*), which gave the sonnet a violence it had perhaps always contained but had never been asked to display.

---

In February, they opened the bay outside the seminar room, and the smell came in: a deep cellar smell of things sealed away for half a century, and under it something sharper, chemical. The foreman explained it was the primer for the membrane, perfectly safe once cured.

"And before it's cured?" Helen asked.

The foreman's name was Tomasz. He was a broad, careful man with reading glasses pushed up into his gray hair, and he looked at her as if he had been asked this before, by other people who worked in rooms full of paper.

"Before it's cured," he said, "open a window."

"The windows are covered in plastic."

"Yes," Tomasz said. "That's a problem."

Helen came to like him, the way one likes a doctor who delivers bad news plainly. He left a box of N95 masks on the department counter without comment. Once, passing her office, he looked at the bloomed shelf she had not been able to throw away and shook his head slowly, as if at a grave.

Marguerite Tessier, who worked on Racine and had asthma, began to cough in March and did not stop. She carried an air-quality monitor from room to room like a priest with a censer, reading out the numbers in a voice of grim triumph. An industrial hygienist reported that the levels were "elevated but within occupational limits." Marguerite pointed out that those limits were designed for construction workers, not people who sat nine hours a day reading Phèdre. The hygienist said he would look into it. He did not come back.

The department fractured along lines that had always been there, like hairline cracks in the concrete. At the April meeting, Marguerite accused Peter of complicity. Arnold accused Marguerite of hysteria. A junior colleague who worked on Brazilian modernism said nothing, staring at the table like someone calculating how long until she could reasonably leave.

Helen belonged to no faction. Outrage seemed to her a fuel that burned too fast. Institutions moved at the speed of rain through concrete, and shouting at them was like shouting at weather.

---

August came, and the project was not finished. The colored bars had slid rightward like books on a shelf when a bookend is removed. The rebar repair had uncovered "significantly more" corrosion, Tomasz said, in the tone of a surgeon who has found the tumor larger than the scans suggested. The new completion date was the following May.

Peter read the email aloud at the September meeting. No one said anything. Marguerite was on medical leave, her face on the screen at the end of the table, a reproach in a rectangle. Arnold had announced his retirement. The young woman who worked on Brazilian modernism had an offer from California, and everyone knew it, and no one mentioned it.

Afterward, Helen sat at her desk. The plastic over the windows had been replaced with a heavier grade, faintly blue, and the light was the color of shallow water. She took down the ruined Vieira. It was lighter than she remembered; the mold had dried and gone gray. She found she couldn't throw it away, so she put it back and began reading her lecture notes for the morning.

---

In late October, Tomasz knocked on her door.

"You want to see something?"

She followed him up a ladder and through a hatch onto the scaffolding outside the north face. The wind was cold. Below, the quad was yellow with leaves. Tomasz led her to an open bay where the panels had been removed and the raw structure stood exposed, scarred and patched and gray, and over it, smooth and black and faintly gleaming, lay the membrane.

It was beautiful, the way ordinary things are beautiful when you have waited a long time for them. It looked like a still pond at night. It looked like a closed eye.

"Three-eighths of an inch," Tomasz said. "Like the drawings."

Helen touched it. It was cool and slightly tacky, and it gave a little under her fingers, the way skin does.

"Fifty-four years," she said.

"Fifty-five, by the time we're done," Tomasz said. "Maybe fifty-six."

She stood there, the wind pulling at her coat, and thought of the rain that would fall on the building that winter and all the winters after, long after she and Tomasz and the young woman bound for California were gone. Rain that would seep inward and meet, at last, this thin dark layer, and stop, and turn back, and run down to the ground the way it had always been meant to. It seemed to her a small thing, and also not small at all.

"Okay," she said. "Okay."

Then she climbed back down and returned to her office, with its blue light and its ticking clock and its shelf of ruined books, and sat down to wait for spring.
